# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy for Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a major global health burden, affecting more than 25 million people worldwide despite advances in guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) [1]. Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) has transformed outcomes for selected patients, but the majority of patients with HF have a narrow QRS duration and are therefore ineligible [2]. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) has emerged to fill this therapeutic gap. CCM involves the delivery of a train of high-amplitude, biphasic electrical impulses during the absolute refractory period of the cardiac cycle that alter intracellular calcium handling, resulting in an increase in myocardial contractility without an associated increase in oxygen consumption [3].

## Mechanisms of Action

The defining feature of CCM is that the delivered signal is "non-excitatory": it does not initiate a new action potential. CCM delivers an electrical current during the absolute refractory period, 30 to 40 milliseconds after detection of local myocardial activation and without generating an action potential or cellular contraction [4]. Mechanistic studies have illuminated how this augments contractility. At the cellular level, in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, CCM therapy has been shown to restore calcium handling and improve the metabolic status of cardiac myocytes, reverse the heart failure-associated fetal gene program, and reduce the extent of interstitial fibrosis [5]. Proposed mechanisms for the increase in cytoplasmic calcium include increased activation and duration of opening of ryanodine receptors, increased calcium influx via the L-type calcium channel, and increased calcium influx into the sarcoplasmic reticulum via SERCA2a [6]. Reduced SERCA2a expression and activity is a hallmark of the failing heart, making it a logical target [7]. Canine HF studies demonstrated that therapy with CCM electrical signals improves left ventricular function and remodeling in dogs with chronic heart failure [8], and that CCM electrical signals improve myocardial gene expression in patients with heart failure [9]. Critically, unlike cAMP-dependent positive inotropic drugs, the increase in LV function during CCM therapy is elicited without increasing myocardial oxygen consumption [10], and the molecular effects extend to right ventricular and diastolic function [11].

## Clinical Trial Evidence

The first major randomized data came from the European FIX-CHF-4 study. Borggrefe and colleagues performed a randomized, double-blind, crossover study in which 164 subjects with ejection fraction below 35% and NYHA class II or III symptoms received a CCM pulse generator [12], demonstrating improved exercise tolerance and quality of life [13]. In the United States, the pivotal FIX-HF-5 trial followed. CCM was tested in 428 NYHA class III or IV, narrow QRS HF patients with ejection fraction ≤35% randomized to optimal medical therapy plus CCM versus optimal medical therapy alone; efficacy was assessed by ventilatory anaerobic threshold, peak VO2, and the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire, and the primary safety endpoint was a noninferiority test for the composite of all-cause mortality and hospitalizations [14]. The study met its primary safety endpoint but did not reach its primary efficacy endpoint; however, in a prespecified subgroup analysis, significant improvements in primary and secondary endpoints were observed in patients with ejection fractions ranging from 25% to 45% [15,16].

This subgroup signal was confirmed in the FIX-HF-5C trial. A total of 160 patients with NYHA class III or IV symptoms, QRS duration below 130 ms, and ejection fraction between 25% and 45% were randomized to control or CCM for 24 weeks, with the difference in peak VO2 between groups of 0.84 mL O2/kg/min satisfying the primary endpoint [17]. A subsequent two-lead system was evaluated in FIX-HF-5C2. The new 2-lead system eliminated the need for an atrial lead and was shown to effectively deliver comparable CCM signals—including in subjects with atrial fibrillation—while being equally safe and improving peak VO2 and NYHA class [18]. A comprehensive individual patient data meta-analysis reinforced these findings: a meta-analysis of all non-confounded prospective randomized controlled trials of CCM versus control measured functional capacity and quality of life in patients with HF [19], showing significant improvements in peak VO2, six-minute walk distance, and quality of life [20].

## Long-Term Outcomes and Registries

Beyond functional endpoints, registry and observational data suggest possible prognostic benefit. Anker and colleagues reported that CCM improves long-term survival and hospitalizations in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction [21]. The CCM-REG registry, a prospective study including 503 patients from 51 European centres, evaluated effects across terciles of LVEF and in patients with atrial fibrillation and normal sinus rhythm [22], and other long-term single-center series have shown sustained clinical improvement and reduced HF hospitalizations [23,24]. Imaging studies corroborate reverse remodeling: CCM improves both global and regional LV contractility, including regions remote from the impulse delivery, and may contribute to LV reverse remodeling and gain in systolic function [25].

## Atrial Fibrillation and Expanding Indications

Recent US FDA labeling of CCM therapy specifically removed the requirement for normal sinus rhythm, so CCM can now be offered to patients with HFrEF who are in atrial fibrillation [26]. Feasibility in permanent AF was demonstrated even before the two-lead system became available [27]. Interest is also expanding toward higher ejection fractions and HFpEF [28]. A pilot study (CCM-HFpEF) demonstrated that the benefits of CCM may extend to the HFpEF population, with significant improvement in health status and no obvious impact on safety [29]. The current AIM HIGHer randomized trial is evaluating CCM in HFmrEF/HFpEF.

## Guidelines and Conclusion

The OPTIMIZER Smart System received FDA approval in 2019 [30]. Within contemporary practice, CCM occupies a defined niche for symptomatic HFrEF patients with narrow QRS who are not CRT candidates, offering improvements in exercise tolerance, symptoms, and quality of life. Definitive mortality data and confirmation of benefit in HFpEF await ongoing randomized trials.
